clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of cholesterol efflux caused by variants in ABCA1, producing very low high-density lipoprotein and low total cholesterol with near-absent apolipoprotein A-I
Cholesteryl ester accumulates in the reticuloendothelial system, giving the hallmark enlarged orange or yellow-grey tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy

Peripheral neuropathy is a defining feature and takes two main forms: a relapsing-remitting multifocal (mononeuritis multiplex-like) neuropathy and a slowly progressive syringomyelia-like pattern with dissociated sensory loss
The pseudosyringomyelic form causes loss of pain and temperature sensation with relative sparing of light touch and proprioception, mimicking a central cord lesion
A markedly low HDL cholesterol in a patient with neuropathy and prominent tonsils should prompt consideration of Tangier disease
Despite low overall cholesterol, patients have an increased risk of premature atherosclerotic vascular disease because protective HDL is deficient
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic lipid profile and clinical features, confirmed by ABCA1 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Tangier disease is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ABCA1, a transporter that mediates the efflux of cellular cholesterol and phospholipid onto lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I to form nascent high-density lipoprotein. Without functional ABCA1, apolipoprotein A-I is not lipidated and is rapidly catabolised, so plasma HDL and apolipoprotein A-I fall to very low levels and total cholesterol is reduced. Unesterified cholesterol and cholesteryl esters accumulate within macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system, producing the enlarged orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and foam-cell infiltration. Lipid accumulation within Schwann cells and nerves is thought to underlie the demyelinating and axonal neuropathy, which can be multifocal and relapsing or produce a syringomyelia-like dissociated sensory loss.
additionalDifferentials: Analphalipoproteinaemia and other severe HDL-deficiency states
Syringomyelia and other intramedullary cord lesions
Leprous neuropathy with dissociated sensory loss
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid panel showing very low HDL cholesterol, low total cholesterol and reduced apolipoprotein A-I
ABCA1 sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Nerve conduction studies characterising the multifocal or sensory-predominant neuropathy
Nerve biopsy showing lipid-laden Schwann cells in selected cases
Examination and imaging of tonsils, liver and spleen for lipid deposition
Cardiovascular risk assessment given the predisposition to atherosclerosis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or severe multifocal neuropathy causing functional loss
Symptoms of premature coronary or cerebrovascular disease
Progressive dissociated sensory loss raising concern for a cord lesion needing imaging
Painless injuries or burns from unrecognised pain and temperature loss
reference.prognosis: The neuropathy may relapse and remit or slowly progress and can cause substantial disability; long-term outlook is also influenced by an increased risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
pitfalls: Overlooking a very low HDL as a clue and attributing neuropathy to a more common cause
Mistaking the pseudosyringomyelic sensory loss for a primary spinal cord lesion
Assuming low total cholesterol is protective and neglecting cardiovascular risk
Failing to examine the tonsils, which show the characteristic orange discolouration
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
